p.src: This lyric is set to the tune “Su Wu Man.” Now the story tells how our Buddha, the Tathagata, took leave of the Jade Emperor and returned to the precious monastery of Thunderclap. There he saw the three thousand Buddhas, five hundred Arhats, eight Great Vajra Guardians, and countless Bodhisattvas, each bearing banners, canopies, rare treasures, and celestial flowers, arrayed beneath the twin sal trees in the immortal precincts of Spirit Mountain to welcome him. The Tathagata halted his auspicious cloud and addressed the assembly: “With profound prajna I have surveyed the Three Realms throughout. The original nature at its root is, in the final reckoning, quiescent extinction. It is like empty space, possessing nothing whatsoever. The subjugation of the wayward monkey is a matter beyond ordinary knowing. From naming arise birth and death; such is the true aspect of the Dharma.” When he had finished, he emitted the radiance of his relics; forty-two white rainbows filled the sky, stretching from south to north. At the sight, the whole assembly bowed down in reverence. Presently, gathering clouds of felicity and rainbow mist around him, he ascended the highest lotus throne and sat there in serene dignity. The three thousand Buddhas, five hundred Arhats, eight Vajra Guardians, and four Bodhisattvas approached with palms joined, paid their respects, and asked, “What became of the one who caused havoc in the Celestial Palace and disrupted the Peach Banquet?” The Tathagata replied, “That rogue was a demon monkey born on the Mountain of Flowers and Fruit. His crimes towered to Heaven and defied description. Not one of all the celestial generals could subdue him. Though Erlang captured him and Lord Lao refined him in fire, even that could do him no harm. When I arrived, he was in the midst of the thunder generals, flaunting his might and displaying his prowess. I stopped the fighting and questioned him about his origins. He claimed to possess divine powers and transformations, and to ride a Somersault Cloud that carried him one hundred and eight thousand li in a single leap. I made a wager with him. When he failed to escape my palm, I seized him, transformed my fingers into the Five Elements Mountain, and sealed him beneath it. The Jade Emperor opened wide the Golden Portal and Jasper Palace, seated me in the place of honor, and held a Great Banquet for the Pacification of Heaven to thank me. Only then did I take leave and return.” The assembly rejoiced at these words and praised him to the utmost.

p.src: The Buddha dwelt in the precious monastery of Great Thunderclap on Spirit Mountain. One day he summoned the Buddhas, Arhats, Jiedi Guardians, Bodhisattvas, Vajra Guardians, monks, nuns, and the rest, and said, “Since the wayward ape was subdued and Heaven pacified, we here have lost all count of months and years; I reckon that five hundred years have passed in the mortal world. Today is the full moon of the first autumn month. I possess a precious basin filled with a hundred rare flowers, a thousand wondrous fruits, and other delicacies. What say you to sharing this Ullambana Feast with me?” One and all joined their palms, circled the Buddha three times in reverence, and accepted his invitation. The Tathagata then had Ananda hold the flowers, fruits, and delicacies from the precious basin while Kasyapa distributed them. Filled with gratitude, the assembly each presented a poem in thanks.

p.src: When the Tathagata had finished preaching, he said to the assembly, “I have observed the Four Great Continents, and the goodness and wickedness of their living beings differ from region to region. In the Eastern Continent of Superior Deity, they revere Heaven and honor Earth, and their hearts are clear and their tempers peaceful. In the Northern Continent of Kuru, though they are fond of killing, they kill only to fill their bellies; being simple by nature and unrefined in feeling, they commit little wanton cruelty. In our Western Continent of Cattle-Gift, they neither covet nor kill, but nurture their vital breath and conceal their spiritual power. Though they have no supreme immortals, everyone enjoys a secure longevity. But in the Southern Continent of Jambu, they are greedy and lustful, delight in calamity, and abound in killing and strife. It is truly a murderous arena of vicious tongues, a wicked sea of quarrels and blame. I now possess the true scriptures of the Three Baskets, which can exhort people to goodness.” Hearing this, the Bodhisattvas joined their palms and took refuge, then asked before the Buddha, “Which true scriptures of the Three Baskets does the Tathagata possess?” The Tathagata said, “I have one basket of Dharma, which speaks of Heaven; one basket of Treatises, which speaks of Earth; and one basket of Sutras, which delivers ghosts. Together the Three Baskets comprise thirty-five divisions and fifteen thousand one hundred and forty-four scrolls. They are scriptures for cultivating truth and the gateway to upright goodness. I would send them to the Eastern Land, but unfortunately its people are foolish: they slander the true words, fail to understand the essential purport of my Dharma gate, and slight the orthodox teaching of Yoga. If only someone with divine power would go to the Eastern Land and find a devout believer, bid him endure the hardships of a thousand mountains and seek the scriptures across ten thousand rivers, until he comes here to obtain the true scriptures and transmit them forever in the East, converting its living beings to goodness. That would indeed be a blessed affinity as great as a mountain and a fortunate deed as deep as the sea. Who is willing to make the journey?” At once the Bodhisattva Guanyin approached the lotus throne, circled the Buddha three times in reverence, and said, “Though this disciple is unworthy, I am willing to go to the Eastern Land and find a pilgrim to fetch the scriptures.” The whole assembly raised their heads to behold the Bodhisattva:

p.src: The Tathagata was overjoyed to see her and said, “No one else could undertake this journey. Only the Venerable Guanyin, whose divine powers are vast, is capable of going.” The Bodhisattva said, “What instructions have you for this disciple on my journey to the Eastern Land?” The Tathagata replied, “On this journey you must examine the road itself; you are not permitted to travel high through the firmament. You must travel half in cloud and half in mist, surveying the mountains and rivers with your own eyes. Carefully remember the distances along the route so that you may instruct the scripture pilgrim. But fearing that the devout believer may find the journey difficult, I shall give you five treasures.” He immediately ordered Ananda and Kasyapa to bring out a brocade kasaya robe. They also brought a nine-ringed priest’s staff, and he said to the Bodhisattva, “This kasaya and staff are for the personal use of the scripture pilgrim. If he is resolved to come here, wearing my kasaya will save him from falling into the cycle of rebirth; and bearing my staff will protect him from poisonous harm.” The Bodhisattva bowed in devotion and accepted them. The Tathagata then brought out three circlets and handed them to the Bodhisattva, saying, “These treasures are called binding circlets. Though all three look alike, each has a different use. I have three spells: the Golden, the Binding, and the Prohibitive. If on the road you encounter a demon of great divine power, you must exhort him to mend his ways and become a disciple of the scripture pilgrim. If he refuses to submit and obey, place one of these circlets upon his head; it will naturally take root in his flesh. Recite the spell suited to that circlet, and his eyes will swell, his head will ache, and his very skull will seem to split. That will surely make him enter my gate.”

p.src: Hearing this, the monster repeatedly murmured assent and lowered his precious staff. He let Mucha lead him before Guanyin, where he bowed his head to the ground and pleaded, “Bodhisattva, forgive my offense and hear my story. I am no evil demon, but was once the Curtain-Raising General who attended the imperial chariot below the Hall of Divine Mist. Only because I accidentally smashed a crystal goblet at the Peach Banquet, the Jade Emperor had me struck eight hundred times and banished me to the lower world, where I took on this appearance. He also ordered a flying sword to come every seventh day, pierce my chest and sides more than a hundred times, and only then withdraw. That is why I suffer so bitterly. With no other recourse, and unable to endure hunger and cold, every few days I emerge from the waves to find a traveler to eat. In my ignorance today, I unexpectedly offended the greatly compassionate Bodhisattva.” The Bodhisattva said, “You committed a crime in Heaven and were banished; now you take life in this fashion, adding sin upon sin. I have received the Buddha’s command to go to the Eastern Land and seek the scripture pilgrim. Why not enter my gate, take refuge in the good fruition, become that pilgrim’s disciple, and journey to the Western Heaven to worship the Buddha and seek the scriptures? I shall stop the flying sword from piercing you. When the task is accomplished, your crime will be remitted and your former office restored. What do you say?” The monster replied, “I am willing to embrace the true fruition.” Then he stepped forward and said, “Bodhisattva, I have eaten countless people here. Several scripture pilgrims have come this way before, and I ate them all. Whenever I cast an eaten man’s head into the River of Flowing Sands, it sank straight to the bottom. Not even a goose feather can float on this water. Only the skulls of nine scripture pilgrims floated on the surface and would not sink. Thinking them strange objects, I strung them together on a cord and play with them in my idle hours. But if I remain here and the scripture pilgrim never comes this way, will that not ruin my prospects instead?” The Bodhisattva said, “How could he possibly fail to come? Hang the skulls around your neck and await the scripture pilgrim; they will serve a purpose in due course.” The monster said, “If that is so, I shall gladly accept your instruction.” The Bodhisattva then laid a hand upon his head and administered the precepts. Taking the sand as his surname, she gave him the surname Sha; and gave him the religious name Sha Wujing. Having entered the Buddhist order, he escorted the Bodhisattva across the river. Thereafter he cleansed his heart and thoughts, harmed no more living creatures, and devoted himself to awaiting the scripture pilgrim.

p.src: Just as the two were fighting at their fiercest, Guanyin cast down a lotus from midair and parted rake from staff. The monster was startled at the sight and asked, “What monastery are you from, monk, that you dare conjure such tricks before my eyes to fool me?” Mucha said, “You wretched creature of fleshly eyes and mortal clay! I am a disciple of the Bodhisattva of the Southern Sea. That lotus was cast by my master, and still you fail to recognize it!” The monster asked, “By the Bodhisattva of the Southern Sea, do you mean Guanyin, who sweeps away the Three Calamities and delivers beings from the Eight Adversities?” Mucha replied, “Who else could it be?” The monster threw down his rake, bowed his head to the ground, and said, “Brother, where is the Bodhisattva? Please trouble yourself to introduce me.” Mucha looked up and pointed. “Is that not she?” The monster kowtowed toward the sky and cried loudly, “Bodhisattva, forgive me! Forgive me!”

I was originally Marshal Tianpeng of the River of Heaven. Only because I drank too much and made improper advances to Chang’e, the Jade Emperor had me struck two thousand times with a mallet and banished me to the mortal dust. My true spirit went straight to seize a body and enter a womb, but by mischance took the wrong road and entered the womb of a sow, leaving me in this form. I bit the sow to death, killed the whole herd of swine, occupied this mountain, and have lived here by eating people. Now that I have unexpectedly encountered you, Bodhisattva, I beg you to save me.” The Bodhisattva asked, “What is this mountain called?” The monster replied, “It is called Mount Fuling. There is a cave in the mountain called Cloud Pathway Cave. A woman called Second Elder Sister Egg once lived there. Seeing that I possessed some martial skill, she took me as head of her household—that is, as a live-in son-in-law. Before a year had passed, she died, and all the property in the cave fell to my enjoyment. I have lived here for many years, and having no trade by which to support myself, I have simply followed my old habit of living on human flesh. I earnestly beg the Bodhisattva to forgive my sins.” The Bodhisattva said, “The ancients said, ‘If you desire a future, do nothing that destroys your future.’ You broke the law in the upper realm, and now, failing to reform your savage heart, you kill living beings and create evil karma. Will you not be punished for both crimes?” The monster said, “A future, a future! If I obey you, am I to live on air? As the common saying goes, ‘Obey the law and be beaten to death; obey the Buddha’s law and starve to death.’ Enough, enough! Better to catch some traveler and feast richly on his flesh. What do I care for two sins or three, a thousand or ten thousand!” The Bodhisattva said, “‘When a person cherishes a good resolve, Heaven will surely grant it.’ If you are willing to take refuge in the true fruition, you will naturally have the means to sustain yourself. The world has five grains with which hunger may be relieved. Why must you live by eating people?”

p.src: At these words the monster seemed to awaken from a dream and said to the Bodhisattva, “I wish to follow the right path, but ‘when one has offended Heaven, there is nowhere one can pray.’” The Bodhisattva said, “I have received the Buddha’s command to go to the Eastern Land and seek the scripture pilgrim. You may become his disciple and journey with him to the Western Heaven. By redeeming your crime through meritorious service, you will assuredly be delivered from your afflictions.” The monster eagerly replied, “I will follow him! I will follow him!” The Bodhisattva then laid a hand upon his head and administered the precepts. Taking his body as the basis for his surname, she gave him the surname Zhu; and gave him the religious name Zhu Wuneng. Thus he accepted the command and returned to the true path, keeping a vegetarian fast, abstaining from the five pungent plants and the three forbidden meats, and devoting himself to awaiting the scripture pilgrim.

p.src: The Bodhisattva and Muzha took their leave of Wuneng and journeyed onward, half borne upon cloud and mist. As they went, they suddenly saw a jade dragon crying out in midair. The Bodhisattva drew near and asked, “What dragon are you, that you suffer punishment here?” The dragon replied, “I am the son of Ao Run, Dragon King of the Western Sea. Because I carelessly set fire to a bright pearl in the palace, my royal father submitted a memorial to Heaven accusing me of disobedience. The Jade Emperor had me hung in the air and given three hundred strokes, and before long I am to be executed. I beg the Bodhisattva to save me!”

p.src: When Guanyin heard this, she and Muzha went straight through the Southern Gate of Heaven, where Celestial Masters Qiu and Zhang were already waiting to receive them and asked, “Where are you bound?” The Bodhisattva said, “This poor cleric wishes to see the Jade Emperor.” The two Celestial Masters hastened to report her arrival. The Jade Emperor then descended from his throne to welcome her. After stepping forward and making her obeisance, the Bodhisattva said, “By the Buddha’s decree, this poor cleric is traveling to the Eastern Land to seek a scripture pilgrim. On my way I encountered a sinful dragon hanging in punishment. I have come especially to petition Your Majesty to spare his life and grant him to me, so that he may serve as a mount for the scripture pilgrim.” Hearing this, the Jade Emperor immediately issued a decree of pardon, ordering a heavenly general to release the dragon and deliver him to the Bodhisattva. The Bodhisattva gave thanks for the imperial favor and departed. The young dragon kowtowed in gratitude for his life and submitted himself to the Bodhisattva’s commands. The Bodhisattva placed him in a deep ravine to await the scripture pilgrim, when he was to turn into a white horse and win merit on the journey west. The young dragon accepted the command and concealed himself beneath the waters; of him we speak no more for now.

p.src: The Bodhisattva led the pilgrim Muzha over the mountain and continued toward the Eastern Land. Before they had gone far, they suddenly beheld ten thousand shafts of golden light and a thousand streams of auspicious vapor. Muzha said, “Master, the place giving off that light is the Five Elements Mountain. The Tathagata’s sealing inscription is still there.” The Bodhisattva said, “Then this is where the Great Sage Equaling Heaven, who disrupted the Peach Banquet and wreaked havoc in the Celestial Palace, is now pinned down.” Muzha said, “Indeed he is, indeed he is.” Master and disciple climbed the mountain together and examined the inscription. p.src: As master and disciple were speaking, they had already roused the Great Sage. From beneath the foot of the mountain, the Great Sage shouted, “Who is up there reciting poetry and exposing my shame?” Hearing him, the Bodhisattva went straight down the mountain to investigate. Beneath a rocky cliff she found the local earth god, the mountain god, and the heavenly generals guarding the Great Sage. They all came to bow in welcome and led the Bodhisattva before him. When she looked, she saw that he was pinned inside a stone casket: his mouth could speak, but his body could not move. The Bodhisattva said, “You there, Sun—do you recognize me?” The Great Sage opened his Fiery Eyes and Golden Pupils, nodded, and cried aloud, “How could I fail to recognize you? p.src: When the Bodhisattva heard these words, her heart filled with joy, and she said to the Great Sage, “The sacred classic says, ‘Speak words of goodness, and people a thousand miles away will respond; speak words that are not good, and people a thousand miles away will oppose them.’ Since you possess such resolve, wait until I reach the Great Tang realm in the Eastern Land and find a scripture pilgrim; I shall have him come and release you. You may become his disciple, uphold the teaching and its discipline, enter the fold of our Buddha, and cultivate yourself anew until you attain the true fruit. What do you say?” Again and again the Great Sage cried, “I will go! I will go!” The Bodhisattva said, “Since you have planted this good seed, I shall give you a religious name.” The Great Sage said, “I already have a name. I am called Sun Wukong.” The Bodhisattva rejoiced again and said, “The two who submitted to me earlier also belong to the generation whose names bear the character ‘Wu.’ Since yours bears ‘Wu’ as well, you match them perfectly. Excellent, excellent! Then there is no need for further instruction. I shall go now.” The Great Sage perceived his true nature, awakened his mind, and returned to the Buddha’s teaching; the Bodhisattva kept her purpose firmly in mind as she sought the holy monk.

p.src: She and Muzha left that place and traveled straight east. Before many days had passed, they reached Chang’an in the Great Tang realm. Drawing in their mist and gathering up their clouds, master and disciple transformed themselves into two scabby wandering monks and entered the city of Chang’an. Before they knew it, evening had fallen. Reaching the side of the main market street, they saw a shrine to the local earth god and went straight inside. The local earth god was frightened into a panic, and his ghostly soldiers trembled with fear. Realizing that the visitor was the Bodhisattva, he kowtowed and welcomed her inside. The earth god then hurried to report to the city god, the gods of the soil, and all the deities of every temple throughout Chang’an. When they learned that it was the Bodhisattva, they came to pay their respects and said, “Bodhisattva, forgive us gods for receiving you so late.” The Bodhisattva said, “You must not let the slightest word of this leak out. By the Buddha’s decree, I have come especially to this place to seek a scripture pilgrim. Lend me your temple so that I may stay here a few days. Once I have found the true monk, I shall return.” The gods each returned to their own places, driving the local earth god to lodge temporarily in the city god’s temple, while the Bodhisattva and her disciple concealed their true forms.
